text.en: ALTK-Evolve learns and applies a playbook using GPT-4.1, outperforming the retail entries on τ²-bench, a customer service agent benchmark—without updating model weights.

text.en: Learned memory takes a basic ReAct agent with GPT-4.1 to the top
text.th: Learned memory takes a basic ReAct agent with GPT-4.1 to the top

text.en: Using GPT-4.1, an older, non-reasoning model, a basic customer-service agent reaches 67.5% Pass^4 on τ²-bench retail — meaning it solves the task on all four independent attempts for 67.5% of tasks. It scores above every retail entry in our October 12, 2026 leaderboard snapshot. It runs on the benchmark's stock ReAct scaffold, with learned guidelines appended to its system prompt.
text.th: Using GPT-4.1, an older, non-reasoning model, a basic customer-service agent reaches 67.5% Pass^4 on τ²-bench retail — meaning it solves the task on all four independent attempts for 67.5% of tasks. It scores above every retail entry in our October 12, 2026 leaderboard snapshot. It runs on the benchmark's stock ReAct scaffold, with learned guidelines appended to its system prompt.

text.en: ALTK-Evolve builds that playbook using GPT-4.1. It analyzes the agent's training-task attempts and uses the model to distill successes and failures into short behavioral rules: how to authenticate a customer, confirm a transaction, or handle a return. Those guidelines are then added to the agent's prompt for subsequent conversations. The same model powers both guideline extraction and the agent; no weight updates or human annotation are needed.

text.en: Our previous work demonstrated this approach on coding agents. Here, we test it on customer service, where success requires following domain policies, understanding a customer's request, and executing the right tool actions.

text.en: τ²-bench tests policy-bound customer service
text.th: τ²-bench tests policy-bound customer service

text.en: τ²-bench (from Sierra) measures how well an agent handles customer-service conversations under real constraints. Each task pairs the agent with an LLM-simulated customer who has a goal in mind, a set of domain tools (look up an order, issue a refund, rebook a flight), and a written policy document the agent must follow. The agent has to draw out the right details, stay within policy, and take the correct — often irreversible — actions; a task counts as solved only when the final database state matches the expected outcome, a strict binary reward. We use its two customer-service domains, retail and airline.
text.th: τ²-bench (from Sierra) measures how well an agent handles customer-service conversations under real constraints. Each task pairs the agent with an LLM-simulated customer who has a goal in mind, a set of domain tools (look up an order, issue a refund, rebook a flight), and a written policy document the agent must follow. The agent has to draw out the right details, stay within policy, and take the correct — often irreversible — actions; a task counts as solved only when the final database state matches the expected outcome, a strict binary reward. We use its two customer-service domains, retail and airline.

text.en: We run τ²-bench's own implementation of a basic ReAct agent with a two-phase THINK → ACT loop, using gpt-4.1 as the agent model and gpt-5.5 as the customer-simulator model; 4 trials per task. The only change we make is a block of learned guidelines appended to the system prompt — everything else (policy, tools, scaffold) is stock τ²-bench. Concretely, the learned guidelines are tacked on after the domain policy as a plain markdown list:

text.en: We extract guidelines from the agent's trajectories on τ²-bench train tasks using gpt-4.1, the same model that powers the agent, then apply them unchanged on the held-out test set.

text.en: Guidelines improve capability and reliability
text.th: Guidelines improve capability and reliability

text.en: In a prior post, we talked about how different models / tasks require different dosage of guidance. Inline with the idea, we also evaluate different amounts of guidelines provided to the model.
text.th: In a prior post, we talked about how different models / tasks require different dosage of guidance. Inline with the idea, we also evaluate different amounts of guidelines provided to the model.

text.en: Each guideline carries a support count — the number of distinct training tasks it was extracted from, so higher support means a rule that generalized across more tasks rather than a one-off. We compare three configurations: baseline (no guidelines), sup3 (keep only guidelines with support ≥ 3 — a small, high-confidence core), and lossless (keep every guideline retained after consolidation, i.e. support ≥ 1).
text.th: Each guideline carries a support count — the number of distinct training tasks it was extracted from, so higher support means a rule that generalized across more tasks rather than a one-off. We compare three configurations: baseline (no guidelines), sup3 (keep only guidelines with support ≥ 3 — a small, high-confidence core), and lossless (keep every guideline retained after consolidation, i.e. support ≥ 1).

text.en: Mean Accuracy — the average success rate across the 4 trials. This is the capability axis: how often does the agent get this right?
text.th: Mean Accuracy — the average success rate across the 4 trials. This is the capability axis: how often does the agent get this right?

text.en: Pass^4 — the percentage of tasks that passed across all 4 trials. This measures along the reliability axis and the metric the τ²-bench leaderboard reports. It matters here because a support agent that resolves a refund 3 times out of 4 still fails a quarter of real customers — Pass^4 asks whether you can trust the agent every time, not just on average.

text.en: Mean Accuracy climbs in both domains — retail +4.4 pts (78.1 → 82.5) and airline +7.5 pts (57.5 → 65.0). Reliability moves further: the strict Pass^4 rises +10 pts in retail (57.5 → 67.5) and +10 pts in airline (35.0 → 45.0). And the gains come from better-informed calls, not longer conversations — we look at conversation length directly in Better performance costs more tokens, not more turns below.

text.en: The best amount of guidance depends on the domain
text.th: The best amount of guidance depends on the domain

text.en: The two domains disagree about how much guidance pays off. In retail, more is better on every metric — the small sup3 core barely beats baseline on accuracy, and you need the full lossless set for the real jump. In airline the picture flips at the reliability end: lossless leads on accuracy (65% vs 60%), but the compact sup3 core (14 guidelines) is the more reliable one, taking Pass^4 to 45% against lossless's 40%. Echoing the earlier finding that delivery is a dial, not a constant, support count is a knob worth tuning per domain, not a value to hard-code.

text.en: Does the agent get there by talking longer? To answer that cleanly we compare like for like: the task runs solved under both baseline and the guideline variant — identical scenario and seed, a true "same task, done right" set — and count assistant turns on each side.

text.en: Table 4. Assistant turns per conversation for matched runs solved under both settings on the test split, pooling four trials.
text.th: Table 4. Assistant turns per conversation for matched runs solved under both settings on the test split, pooling four trials.

text.en: The agent isn't talking longer — on the shared set, guidelines make conversations slightly shorter: lossless trims ~0.3–0.4 turns in both domains (retail 10.59 → 10.16, airline 9.15 → 8.82), and no variant lengthens them. That matters beyond cost: each turn is a sequential LLM round-trip, so fewer turns means lower end-to-end latency — a faster time-to-completion for the customer, not just a cheaper one. The only real price is on the input side — the larger system prompt riding on every LLM call: retail's 292-guideline prompt pushes cost from ~$0.084 to ~$0.139 per conversation, while airline's smaller playbook is cheaper. And in production even that is largely reclaimable with prompt caching, since the guideline block is identical across every call.

text.en: So the trade is a favorable one: for a slightly higher input cost (much of it cached away in practice) the agent lands higher accuracy, higher reliability, and lower time-to-completion at once — not the usual quality-for-latency tradeoff, but all three moving the right way together.

text.en: Learned guidelines also improve agents using frontier models
text.th: Learned guidelines also improve agents using frontier models

text.en: So far, we have used an older, non-reasoning model — gpt-4.1. A fair objection is that learned guidelines might have less to add to an agent using a frontier model: maybe they only patch the gaps of a weaker model. So we tested it directly — we reran airline using gpt-5.5 for both the agent and guideline extraction, on the same τ²-bench ReAct scaffold, with guidelines re-mined from the agent's own runs. One detail changes with the model: none of the guidelines extracted in this setup reached support ≥ 3 (they top out at support 2), so the high-support core here is sup2 rather than sup3.

text.en: The learned guidelines improve this setup too. On the same held-out test tasks, appending them to the prompt lifts accuracy +10 pts (72.5 → 82.5) and the strict Pass^4 by +15 pts (55.0 → 70.0) — a larger reliability gain than we observed with gpt-4.1 on these very tasks (+10 pts), and from a much higher floor. Learning guidelines around the model can improve an agent even when it starts from a stronger base. And where the baseline's reliability swung between reruns, the lossless configuration reproduced exactly — the gain it buys is dependable, not a lucky draw.

text.en: Retail: #1. On the base split the agent with learned guidelines reaches Pass^4 = 67.5%, ahead of every frontier model and ahead of RAFT-30B-A3B (61.4%), a model fine-tuned on synthetic τ²-bench retail data. Using stock gpt-4.1 and a prompt-appended playbook, it outperforms that fine-tuned system by +6.1 points.
text.th: Retail: #1. On the base split the agent with learned guidelines reaches Pass^4 = 67.5%, ahead of every frontier model and ahead of RAFT-30B-A3B (61.4%), a model fine-tuned on synthetic τ²-bench retail data. Using stock gpt-4.1 and a prompt-appended playbook, it outperforms that fine-tuned system by +6.1 points.

text.en: Airline: #1 using gpt-5.5, #8 using gpt-4.1 Against the published board, the compact sup3 core gives the agent using gpt-4.1 Pass^4 = 44% — 8th, beating GPT-5.2 (no reasoning) and nearly matching Claude Sonnet 4.5. Swap in the stronger base and the same approach tops the field outright: the agent using gpt-5.5 reaches 82.0%, clearing every frontier entry (66–72%).

text.en: Agents can improve without weight updates
text.th: Agents can improve without weight updates

text.en: Fine-tuning a model on a benchmark is expensive, brittle, and doesn't transfer to the next domain. Here, ALTK-Evolve improves a stock agent on a stock model in both domains — and matches or beats a fine-tuned system on retail — using only prompt-level guidelines extracted from the agent's own runs, automatically, without human annotation, and without any test-set leakage.

Here, ALTK-Evolve improves a stock agent on a stock model in both domains — and matches or beats a fine-tuned system on retail — using only prompt-level guidelines extracted from the agent's own runs, automatically, without human annotation, and without any test-set leakage.
